deep.reconstruction:
This page continues the introduction to E283, which asks how to find a prime larger than any given number. Euler takes up Fermat's proposed answer from the previous page: the numbers F_k = 2^(2^k)+1 are all prime. If that were true, then for any bound N one could take infinitely many powers of two as exponents with 2^n > N and get infinitely many primes above N. Euler says he noticed long ago that the rule is false. The rule holds for every case below 100,000: 3, 5, 17, 257 and 65537. But the very next case, 2^32+1 = 4294967297, is divisible by 641. Since we also do not know whether the larger F_k are prime, the formula gives no help with the problem.

He then separates two questions. Existence is not in doubt: Euclid proved there are infinitely many primes, so infinitely many exceed any given number. Euler adds his own result that the 'multitude' of primes is to the multitude of all numbers as 1 to infinity, or more exactly as log ∞ to ∞, and that ∞ exceeds any power of log ∞. The real problem would be solved by an 'indefinite formula' that produces only primes. He begins to argue (the argument finishes on the next page) that even a formula giving a hundred primes could not be trusted without proof. The next page proves that no polynomial takes only prime values: if A = P(a), then A divides P(nA+a) for every n. In context, the open problem is constructive: produce a prime above N by an explicit rule. That is what the rest of the paper attacks, through primes of special forms such as divisors of a^2+1.
errors: Read literally as a statement about counts, the density claim is wrong. It says the number of primes up to N relates to N as log N relates to N, which would make that count about log N. The truth is about N/log N. The claim is exactly right if 'multitude' is measured by reciprocal sums, as in Euler's E72 (1737): the sum of 1/p up to N is about log log N, while the sum of 1/n is about log N. With x = log N, the ratio is log x : x, which is Euler's phrasing. This is a matter of interpretation rather than an outright error, but it is easily misread as an anticipation of the prime number theorem, and it is not one.

Minor historical simplification: Fermat's stance on whether he had a proof varied across his letters (to Frenicle, Pascal, Digby/Wallis). Euler's 'eo erat candore, ut negaret' reflects some letters but not all.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a well-known historical introduction. It restates the 641 factor (E26), Euclid, and Euler's E72 result on prime 'multitude' in logarithmic language. The only point of interest is that the density remark is exactly right when read through reciprocal sums, and that is already known from E72.
